Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018 - Second Reading - Agree with bill's main idea

Labor opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, which would have drug-tested 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, citing no evidence of effectiveness, opposition from medical and community experts, potential to increase crime and homelessness, and high testing costs.

The speaker supported the government's drug-testing trial for 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, arguing it would identify and help welfare recipients with substance abuse through income management and treatment, with refusal resulting in loss of benefits.

The Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018 would drug test 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients in three locations including Logan, Queensland, but lacks evidence and will harm vulnerable Australians, contrasting with an $80 billion tax handout to big business. No health or community organizations support the trial.

The speaker argued for the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, which would drug test 5,000 new Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah over two years, with a $10 million treatment fund to help those who test positive get clean and into work.

The Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, which would establish drug testing trials for welfare recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Mandurah, and Logan City, was opposed as a punitive and evidence-free measure that would further marginalise vulnerable people, with no expert or community support and undisclosed costs.

The speaker argued that the Drug Testing Trial Bill 2018 should be passed, applying random drug tests to new Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Mandurah and two other trial sites, with positive results leading to income management and referral to treatment. They cited local support, a $10 million boost for drug treatment services, and existing government investments in Mandurah including $2 million for a youth health hub, $581 million for the Tonkin Highway extension, and a drop in unemployment from 11.6% to 6.5%.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is arbitrary, cruel, and lacks evidence, and that drug addiction should be treated as a health issue rather than a punitive measure. They noted the trial would randomly test 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients, with payment cancellation for refusal, and cited opposition from medical experts and community organisations, as well as long waits for rehabilitation.

The speaker argued in favour of the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, which would introduce drug testing for Newstart and youth allowance recipients in trial sites at Logan (Queensland), Mandurah (Western Australia) and Canterbury-Bankstown (New South Wales). The speaker stated the trial is not about punishment but about identifying and supporting people with drug dependencies through counselling, rehabilitation and a $10 million treatment fund, and noted that around 2,500 people would be tested over two years.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it would stigmatise jobseekers, lacked evidence, and was costly, with only 100 to 120 people expected to test positive a second time across the three trial sites in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah.

The speaker argued for the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, a trial of 5,000 people in Canterbury-Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, where Newstart and youth allowance recipients would face drug testing, with first failure leading to 80% of income on a BasicsCard and second failure triggering referral to medical assessment and rehabilitation, funded by $10 million.

Labor opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is based on flawed assumptions and would harm vulnerable people. The party cited evidence from medical and welfare experts, including 982 health professionals, that drug testing welfare recipients is ineffective and costly, with trials in New Zealand and the US returning very few positive results.

The speaker argued for the drug testing trial in the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, describing it as a non-punitive, world-leading measure to break intergenerational welfare dependency and drug addiction, citing 83% coalition voter support and 65% Labor voter support, and referencing the $685 million national ice initiative and $10 million for trial areas.

Centre Alliance maintained its opposition to the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is a rebadged version of a previously rejected bill with no published costings, and citing US evidence that such programs are ineffective and expensive. The party called on parliament to again reject the legislation, stating that existing addiction services are underfunded and that the bill is a populist attempt to demonise welfare recipients.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it would drive up crime and demonise welfare recipients, citing the opposition of a former Australian Federal Police commissioner and the lack of any credible expert support.

The bill introduces a two-year drug testing trial for 5,000 new Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, with income management for positive tests and a $10 million treatment fund. The speaker argued the trial identifies jobseekers with drug abuse issues and helps them access treatment and employment.

This bill would change how student loan debts are repaid and indexed to make the Higher Education Loan Program more sustainable.

It would set new repayment thresholds and rates for HELP loans from 1 July 2018, with a minimum threshold of $45,000 and a one per cent repayment rate, rising to a top threshold of $131,989 at ten per cent.

From 1 July 2019, HELP repayment thresholds would be indexed using the Consumer Price Index instead of Average Weekly Earnings, and from 2019–20, SFSS repayment thresholds would align with HELP thresholds.
Sets new HELP repayment thresholds and rates from 1 July 2018.
Aligns indexation of HELP repayment thresholds to the Consumer Price Index from 1 July 2019.
Brings SFSS repayment thresholds in line with HELP thresholds from 2019–20.
Retains the current three-tier SFSS repayment threshold for 2018–19.
Introduces combined HELP loan limits from 1 January 2020 and allows renewable HELP balances from 2020.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 was introduced to reduce regulatory burden by removing the five-voyage minimum for temporary licences, relaxing tolerance provisions, simplifying consultation requirements, and extending coverage to floating production storage and offloading units and dry-docking vessels. The bill aims to address the expected 30% growth in Australia's freight task by 2030, with coastal shipping currently projected to increase only 15%.

The 2012 Coastal Trading Act failed to halt the decline of Australian shipping, and the 2017 amendment bill should be passed to allow foreign superyachts to charter in Australia by removing customs import duties, which could create 11,800 jobs and $1.64 billion in economic benefit by 2021.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would allow foreign vessels to dominate Australian coastal trade, undermine Australian jobs and wages, and cited that the 2015 bill's regulatory impact statement predicted 1,000 of 1,100 maritime workers would be sacked. They highlighted opposition from the Maritime Union of Australia, Maritime Industry Australia Limited, and the Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers, and referenced the MV Portland and CSL Melbourne incidents where Australian crews were replaced by foreign crews.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would benefit their electorate of Fisher by boosting tourism and economic activity through relaxed superyacht regulations. They cited potential growth in GDP contributions from $590 million to $3.34 billion by 2021 and 8,100 additional jobs, with specific reference to the Mooloolaba Spit and Browns Slipway.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 will decimate seafaring jobs and the maritime industry in Australia. The speaker waited 11 weeks through a gruelling by-election campaign to speak on this bill.

The bill would cause hundreds of Australian seafarer job losses, particularly in Tasmania, by allowing foreign ships and crews to replace Australian vessels on coastal routes, and was developed without consulting the peak shipping industry body, Maritime Industry Australia Ltd.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would accelerate the decline of Australia's merchant fleet and harm national security, environmental protection, and jobs—noting that 12 Australian-flagged vessels have been reflagged under the current government and that the bill's regulatory impact statement explicitly aims to remove barriers for foreign vessels.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 should be passed to remove customs duties and taxes on superyachts, allow temporary licences for round trips, and enable charters, which would generate $1.64 billion and create nearly 12,000 jobs, particularly in Queensland regions like the Whitsundays, Bowen, and Cairns.

The speaker argued against the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, accusing the Liberal Party of seeking to decimate Australian coastal shipping by replacing Australian vessels, workers, and wages with foreign ones. They specifically criticised the member for Dawson for advocating GST removal on vessels worth $100 million while ordinary Australians still pay GST.

The speech opposed the Turnbull government's Coastal Trading Bill, arguing it would destroy Australia's remaining shipping industry and seafarer jobs while favouring foreign vessels, and supported Labor's amendment. It cited the decline to just 12 Australian coastal trading vessels, the Port of Newcastle's 4,600 annual ship movements, and an ACCC investigation into the NSW port privatisation deal.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would decimate Australian shipping jobs and industry, citing that 93% of Australian seafarers could be replaced, over 1,000 jobs lost, and 88% of savings from cheap foreign labour, and criticised changes to tolerance limits and licence variation processes.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would destroy Australian shipping jobs by allowing foreign flag-of-convenience vessels to undercut Australian wages and safety standards, and noted opposition from industry bodies including the Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers, Maritime Industry Australia Ltd, and the Maritime Union of Australia. The speaker also referenced the Howard government's illegal lockout of maritime workers in 1998 as part of a pattern of undermining Australian maritime jobs.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would accelerate the decline of Australia's shipping industry, citing the loss of 12 Australian-flagged vessels since 2013, including the MV Portland. They opposed the bill’s tolerance provisions and licence variation changes, claiming they would disadvantage Australian vessels and workers while favouring foreign operators with lower wages.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would further deregulate and destroy Australia's shipping industry, reducing the fleet from hundreds of vessels in the 1980s to only 11 or 12 today. They claimed this creates national security risks, economic harm, and labour exploitation, citing the loss of Australian-crewed oil tankers, reliance on foreign vessels for fuel, and the live sheep export trade as examples, while opposing the bill in favour of a long-term strategy to revitalise the industry.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would weaken the regulatory framework, harm Australian seafarers, and reduce sovereign self-sufficiency; they noted that Australian flagged ships declined from 55 in 1996 to 21 in 2007 under the Howard government and that no Australian general licensed vessel currently can transport petroleum.

The MP supported the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 but expressed significant concerns about measures including increasing cargo volume tolerance from ±20% to +200%/−100%, expanding loading date tolerance from 5 to 30 days, and halving the time for Australian vessels to apply for temporary licences from 48 hours to 24 hours, arguing these would harm the coastal shipping sector. They also flagged concern over extending the regime to chartered recreational vessels, reserving their party's final position.

The speaker called on the government to withdraw the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it is designed to cut Australian jobs and wages by making it easier for shipowners to replace Australian-flagged vessels and crews with foreign ones. They cited the loss of the Iron Chieftain at Port Kembla, warned of risks to national security and the environment, and criticised the government for dismantling previous Labor reforms that had aimed to rebuild the shipping industry.

Opposing the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, the member for Brand argued it should be withdrawn, citing official modelling that 93 per cent of Australian seafarer jobs would be lost and criticising the government for inadequate consultation. She supported amendments by the member for Grayndler and the member for Whitlam, and defended Labor's 2012 coastal trading reforms against what she described as a repeat of the coalition's failed 2015 attempt.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 was argued to be necessary to reverse the decline of Australia's shipping fleet and workforce caused by decades of neoliberal policies, and to instead use regulation and tax arrangements to increase employment, safety, environmental protection, and revenue.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 simplifies coastal trading regulation, removes the five-voyage minimum for temporary licences, expands coverage to offshore petroleum and superyachts, and reduces red tape to boost efficiency, fuel security, and tourism.

The majority voted against a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2017-05-11.6.2) that would have delayed debate on this bill until 19 August 2019. The majority voted to agree with [the bill's](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr5816%22) main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that they can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill was introduced to tighten the information disclosure requirements for the working holiday maker employer register. Firstly, it will ensure that details of the working holiday maker employer register will not be able to be made publicly available. Secondly, it'll ensure that information sharing between the Australian Tax Office (ATO) and the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) is only undertaken in situations in which an entity is non-compliant, or is reasonably suspected of non-compliance, with a tax law. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd088).

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-19.4.2) to agree with the bill's main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means the Senate can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea?
